title: A Learning Base Camp - A Time for Review
author: Martin Skelton
summary: This is a review post in which Skelton pauses his series to restate, in fifteen numbered statements, the case built so far about what learning is. He argues that learning should be the guiding idea of schools, but that it must be distinguished from the factors that affect it, such as curriculum and teaching, and that a school needs a shared definition of it. Learning is described as a brain process of making neuronal chains sticky through repeated experiences so that we get better. He adds that development differs from learning, that learning has fuzzy boundaries, and that it depends on good struggle across four visible states. He ends by previewing the next stretch, which will treat knowledge, skills and understanding as differently learned, taught and assessed.
points: Skelton claims learning, not curriculum or discipline, should be a school's single guiding concept, since curriculum is only a factor that affects learning.
A school cannot make learning its focus without a shared definition, which he says most schools lack.
His working definition is that learning is a good struggle that hardwires increasingly complex neuronal chains through repeated experience until they become automatic and sticky.
Because the brain is always learning, it picks up unwanted lessons as readily as wanted ones, and the quality and quantity of repeated experiences decide which.
Judging a learner's state requires professional judgement because the boundaries are fuzzy and progress differs by topic.
quotes: For learning to be an organisation’s Hedgehog Concept there has to be a shared agreement about what learning is.
But there is a big difference between the factors that affect learning and learning itself. In other words, curriculum isn’t learning, it’s a factor that affects learning.

Learning is a brain thing. Learning happens in the brain. Our activities - what we do - are factors that affect what and how the brain learns. They aren’t, in themselves, learning. Hence, Are they busy or are they busy learning? (Being just isn’t learning either.)

Learning is about getting better. We can get better in different ways at different things, not all of them good. (We can get better at stealing stuff as well as writing good essays.) But, without getting better at something, there is no learning.
Learning is the process through which we engage in a good struggle to hardwire new and consolidating neuronal chains which, over time and with repeated experiences, become more automatic and sticky.

Learning is dependent upon good struggling. Learning, getting better, is always about moving from somewhere where we were to somewhere where we aren’t, yet. This is not always comfortable. There is always some level of struggle involved.

Equally, children, students and adults alike are likely to be at different places as they learn different things. My ‘consolidating’ learning at ‘x’ is no evidence that I am also consolidating learning at ‘y’. We can’t make simple judgements about our students that apply across the board.
